catalog_quote: Greensmith 1986 p.58: "One reason that I shall not go further into this question is that it may well be a function of stress. A strong stress is discernible in this dialect on the third last syllable of polysyllabic words. Longacre (1957:67) has noted a high pitch on the antepenultimate syllable in contrast to the stress which, he observes, may fall on either the antepenultimate or the penultimate syllables. Although both Wolfart (1973:35) and Pentland (1979:119) mention that stress is far from fully understood, the fact remains that no detailed study has been made. In this study, too, no attempt is made at an analysis of the stress system, as this would have involved work with many informants and the analysis of long passages of text as well as slow elicitation to see how speech style affects the patterning of stress." ... p.115: "In the Woods dialect of Cree, however, stress does not …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding quotations (Greensmith 1986:58 and :115) are verbatim at the stated PDF pages (67, 124) of the held thesis; the p.116 accent-marked transcriptions support antepenultimate placement; the secondary Howse 1844 passage is at pp.297-298 of the held scanned. (2) Deciding source: a 1986 M.A. thesis on segmental variation whose stress remark is impressionistic and hedged ('mostly'; 'no attempt is made at an analysis of the stress system'). It is nonetheless the best Woods-Cree-specific statement I could locate: the Glottolog 'grammar' (Starks 1992, held) is a syntax thesis that defers to Greensmith for phonology and is silent on word-stress placement; Starks 1987a (downloaded now) is silent; Howse 1844 covers emphatic accent only; Glottolog's one 'phonology' entry (Meechan 1999) is misassigned. sources.quote: Plains Cree, not Woods Cree: 'Stress falls regularly on the antepenultimate syllable regardless of whether the word is uninflected or inflected with a prefix and/or suffix(es)... there is no exception to the antepenultimate stress' (p.22-23); surface penultimate stress arises from optional short-vowel elision and glide/h deletion applying after the (postlexical) antepenultimate stress rule. Comparative support for an antepenultimate default across western Cree; explains 'antepenult or penult' surface variation.
sources.locator: p.21 (data: Plains Cree, northern Alberta); sec. 2 'Antepenultimate Stress' pp.22-23; rule ordering pp.27-28

sources.quote: fn.4: 'Bloomfield's statement concerning the occurrence of stress is rather over-simplified: "A non-significant stress accent falls on the third syllable from the end of words or close-knit phrases." Actually a high pitch (part of the unanalyzed intonational system) occurs a good deal more regularly on the antepenultimate syllable than the stress itself which may occur on either the antepenultimate or penultimate syllables.' fn.5: 'the stress seems to fall regularly on the last syllable of disyllabic words'. fn.7: 'stress normally tends to occur in alternating syllables'.
